sentences.text:
Sri Rajeiu Kumar Tripathi, learned counsel for the applicant has submitted that by means of the Government Order dated 21.09.1994, a policy was laid down for establishment of girls high schools/
inter colleges by private managing committees in unserved development blocks.
Policy provided that not less than 3 acres land of gram sabha will be provided to private management bodies free of cost for establishing schools.

In furtherance of the aforesaid policy, the gram sabha concerned had passed a resolution on 30.10.1994 to the effect that the land in question was already recorded in the name of Kisan Inter College, of which the applicant was Manager.
There was no difficulty in transfer of land in the name of Kisan Balika Inter College.

5. On 23.01.1996, another Government Order was issued inter alia providing that the land proved by the Government for establishment of schools will continue to remain in the ownership of the Government and the institution will be a lessee subject to payment of notional premium /lease rent.

6. Sri Rajeiu Kumar Tripathi, learned counsel for the applicant has submitted that by means of another resolution passed by Gaon Sabha on 15.06.1997, it was resolved that another piece of land bearing Gata No.814 measuring 0.34 acre, which was reserved for Khalihan, be also transferred to Kishan Balika Inter College.
7. The applicant claims that in furtherance of the resolution, mutation in the form of Kisan Girls Inter College was carried out in the revenue record.

8. In light of the aforesaid facts, learned counsel for the applicant has submitted that the land in question was duly transferred in the name by Kishan Balika Inter College and, therefore, offences alleged are not made out against the applicant.

9. Per contra Sri Jayant Singh Tomar, the learned A.G.A.-I has vehemently opposed the application and has submitted that there is nothing on record to prima facie indicate that the land in question was actullay transferred to Balika Inter College by any method recognized by law.
He has submitted that the the applicant is guilty of illegally taking into possession government land, for use of a college managed by the applicant.
10. I have considered the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case and the submissions made by learned counsels for the parties.

11. From the submissions made by learned counsel for the applicant himself, prima facie it appears that the State has laid down a policy for transferring lands for establishment of girls high Arif Anwar Hashmi vs State Of U.P. 2 school/intermediate colleges and the policy provided that the lands will be transferred on lease subject to payment of notional premium/lease rent.

entities.text: Arif Anwar Hashmi vs State Of U.P. Thru. Prin. Secy. Home
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is not the case of the applicant that any lease deed was executed in his favour and any amount of premium or lease rent was paid by him.
12. So far as the submission regarding mutation having been carried out in the revenue records is concerned, it is settled law that mutation does not confer right or title in the property.
Right or title can be conferred only by a method recognized by law as per which, a lease of an immovable property for a period of one year, can only be granted through a registered deed.

As no registered lease deed or any other conveyance deed has been executed in favour of the applicant, applicant's claim of having been transferred the land on the basis of mutation entry only, does not merit acceptance by the court.

13. The learned counsel for the applicant has next submitted that even on the basis of allegations leveled in the FIR, offences alleged are not made out as the land in question continues to be in the ownership of the State.

14. Section 2 of Prevention of Damages to Public Property Act, 1984 defines Mischief in Section 2(a)
as "Mischief" shall have the same meaning as in Section 435 of the IPC (45 of 1860).
15. Section 435 IPC reads as follow:-
"425. Mischief.?Whoever with intent to cause, or knowing that he is likely to cause,
wrongful loss or damage to the public or to any person, causes the destruction of any property, or any such change in any property or in the situation thereof as destroys or diminishes its value or utility, or affects it injuriously, commits ?mischief?.
Explanation 1.?It is not essential to the offence of mischief that the offender should intend to cause loss or damage to the owner of the property injured or destroyed.

entities.text: Prevention of Damages to Public Property Act, 1984
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: It is sufficient if he intends to cause, or knows that he is likely to cause, wrongful loss or damage to any person by injuring any property, whether it belongs to that person or not.
Explanation 2.?Mischief may be committed by an act affecting property belonging to the person who commits the act, or to that person and others jointly."

16. Allegations against the applicant are that the institution managed by him has entered into and continues to be in possession of government land since the year 1994 and he has established a school thereon.

Taking possession of Government land and raising a construction thereon prima facie amounts to a change in situation of the property diminishing its utility for the State and having been deprived of possession of the property, State's rights prima facie appear to have been affected injuriously.
Therefore, without going into correctness of the allegations, I am of the view that the allegations prima facie make out a case for commission of the offence of mischief.

17. The learned counsel for the applicant has submitted that for making out an offence of mischief 'intent or knowledge to cause wrongful loss or damage is a sine qua non, which is missing in the present case.

sentences.text: At the stage of considering an application for quashing, the court is not expected to go into minute details of the allegations and the proof thereof.

Prima facie, it cannot be accepted that a person entered upon a Government land without a conveyance deed having been executed in his favour, he raised construction thereon without payment of any consideration to the State and he continued to remain in possession of Government land and to deprive Government of its beneficial uses, without 'intent of causing damage to the government'.
19.
In view of the aforesaid, present application being devoid of merit and substance, is hereby rejected.
